newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan subway cult says it poses no future danger.
newsitem.headline: Japan subway cult says it poses no future danger.

text.p: The religious cult accused of gassing Tokyo subway commuters told a state panel on Monday it poses no future danger to society and should not be outlawed under a draconian anti-subversion law, media reports said.

In the final hearing before the Public Security Commission, an Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect) representative said the cult had not carried out subversive acts in the 19 months since it was raided by police on suspicion of carrying out the March 1995 subway attack, Kyodo news agency said.

The commission, a panel of seven jurists, scholars and media personnel appointed by the justice minister, is expected to rule next month on July's request by the Public Security Investigation Agency that Aum Shinri Kyo be outlawed under a little-used anti-subversion statute.
Since its enactment in 1952, the anti-subversion law has never been invoked, out of concerns that the terms of the law might be said to violate human rights.
If the group were outlawed, members would be banned from holding meetings, producing publications or conducting any other business that would be construed as a group activity.
Cult founder Shoko Asahara and scores of followers are in criminal courts on murder and other charges stemming from the Tokyo subway nerve gas attack, which killed 12 people and made 6,000 ill.
The Public Security Investigation Agency, which operates separately from the commission, has argued that the cult still has fervent followers who pose a danger to society.
In an annual report released last week, the National Police Agency said the cult changed the names of companies it runs and made its followers live together in small groups in apartments.

Acting Aum Shinri Kyo leader Tatsuko Muraoka and a cult lawyer said on Monday that with guru Asahara and all but a few cult officials wanted for the subway attack now in police custody, the sect posed no danger to society, Kyodo reported.

Last week, police unearthed a bottle containing about 40 millilitres (about 1.4 British fluid ounces) of the deadly nerve gas VX after a confession and directions supplied by an incarcerated member of the cult, Yasuo Hayashi, reports said.

Hayashi, a senior member of the sect who was dubbed the "killing machine" by the Japanese media for his suspected involvement in a host of crimes committed by the cult, was arrested early this month with a woman cult member after a year on the run.
Another cultist, Satoru Matsushita, last week directed police to a rural area north of Tokyo where 1.5 kg (3.3 lb) of sodium cyanide -- enough to kill 25,000 people -- was buried, police said.
Matsushita is under arrest on suspicion of helping carry out an abortive cyanide attack on a busy Tokyo train station in May of last year.
Prosecutors have charged Asahara with directing the Tokyo subway attack and involvement in three separate murder and attempted murder cases using VX gas.
Asahara has been accused of 17 separate crimes, but has not entered a plea to any of them.
